name: journal-women-paul-greeted.json
content:
Which women did Paul greet in his letters? Ten, in the last chapter of Romans alone. He names Phoebe, who carried the letter, and Prisca, who risked her neck for him. He names a woman called Junia, whom he places among the apostles in the older reading of the verse. Mary worked hard for the Romans, and Tryphaena, Tryphosa and Persis worked in the Lord. The list closes with Rufus's mother, Julia and the sister of Nereus.1

Set that chapter next to the rule in 1 Timothy that a woman may not teach or hold authority over a man, and you have two Pauls on women. The site makes that case about the letters as a whole. Romans 16 is where it is easiest to see.

Phoebe of Cenchreae

The chapter opens with a letter of recommendation. Paul commends to the Romans "our sister" Phoebe, who serves the church at Cenchreae, the eastern port of Corinth. He asks them to welcome her and help her in whatever she needs, because she has been a patron of many, and of Paul himself.2

Two words in that passage carry the weight. Paul calls her diakonos, the word he uses of himself and of Apollos as servants of God.3 English versions render it servant, minister or deacon. And he calls her prostatis, a patron or protector, a woman with the means to support others. Phoebe held a recognised role in a local church, had money of her own and was trusted to carry Paul's longest letter across the sea.

Prisca and Junia

Prisca comes next, with her husband Aquila. Paul calls them his fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their necks for his life, and says that all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks for them. A church met in their house.4 Paul and Luke both name her before her husband more often than not, and Luke shows her teaching Apollos.5

Then comes the verse that has been fought over for centuries. Paul greets Andronicus and Junia, his kinsmen and fellow prisoners, who were in Christ before him. The Greek says they are episēmoi en tois apostolois.6 The King James Version renders it "of note among the apostles". The ESV renders it as well known to the apostles, which keeps Junia outside the group.

Both readings have scholars behind them. Michael Burer and Daniel Wallace argued for the ESV's sense in 2001.7 Eldon Jay Epp answered them in 2005 with a book titled Junia: The First Woman Apostle.8 The older reading has an early witness. John Chrysostom, preaching on this verse in the late fourth century, praised the devotion of a woman counted worthy of the name of apostle.9 Later editions and translations turned her into a man, "Junias", a name no ancient inscription records. I think Chrysostom read the Greek as its first readers did, but I grant that the grammar alone cannot close the case.

The other Paul

Now the other texts. In 1 Corinthians a woman praying or prophesying must have her head covered.10 The rule assumes that women prayed and prophesied aloud in the assembly. Three chapters later the women are to keep silent in the churches, and if they want to learn anything, to ask their husbands at home.11 The two cannot both describe the same meeting without strain. Gordon Fee argued that the second passage was added to the letter later, partly because some Western manuscripts place it after verse 40 instead.12 Others defend it as Paul's own.

The letter to Timothy is plainer still. A woman is to learn quietly and in full submission. The writer does not allow her to teach or to hold authority over a man, because Adam was formed first, and because the woman, not Adam, was deceived.13 Most critical scholars think 1 Timothy was written in Paul's name a generation or more after him. The church received it as his, and for most of its history it read Romans 16 through it. [paulus_link slug="women-slaves-and-caesar" /] follows that rule into the church's later practice.

So the same name stands over a list of women who served, led and taught, and over a rule that forbids them to teach. [paulus_link slug="the-letters-of-a-man" /] shows that pattern across the letters, and [paulus_link slug="paul-and-the-new-testament" /] explains why a charge against Paul himself rests on the seven letters he certainly wrote, while a charge against the religion may draw on all thirteen.

A Muslim reading

Phoebe, Prisca and Junia were believers who gave their homes, money and safety to the faith as they had received it, and their names have outlived the men who argued over them. I write about them with respect.

The fault lies in the record. A scripture that speaks with two voices on whether half of humanity may teach is a human document, written and edited by people with their own concerns. The 1 Timothy argument also reaches back to Eve as the one deceived. The Qur'an tells the story of the garden differently: Satan whispered to both, both ate, and both turned to God and were forgiven.14 Al-Fārūqī read that account as the end of any inherited sin, for man or woman.15

The Qur'an's rule is single and stated once: "Never will I allow to be lost the work of any worker among you, whether male or female; you are of one another."16 Phoebe at Cenchreae would have recognised it.

The verdict

Romans 16 shows a Paul who works beside women. A deacon carries his letter, a teacher risks her neck for him, and a woman stands among the apostles. Then 1 Timothy, under his name, says a woman may not teach or hold authority over a man.

The two cannot come from one hand and one mind in good faith. Either Paul contradicted himself or somebody wrote in his name. The church has taken the second voice, and it has used it for centuries to close the doors that Romans 16 held open.

The women Paul greeted: questions readers ask

Who was Phoebe in Romans 16?

A woman of the church at Cenchreae, near Corinth, whom Paul calls a diakonos of that church and a patron of many, himself included. She appears to have carried the letter to Rome (Romans 16:1–2).

Was Junia an apostle?

The Greek of Romans 16:7 can mean "of note among the apostles" (KJV) or well known to them (ESV). Chrysostom took her as an apostle. Scholars still divide over the grammar.

Did Paul let women teach?

His undisputed letters show women praying, prophesying and working beside him (1 Corinthians 11:5; Philippians 4:2–3; Romans 16). 1 Timothy 2:12, a letter many scholars think was written in his name, forbids a woman to teach a man.

How many women does Paul greet in Romans 16?

Ten, by name or by relation: Phoebe, Prisca, Mary, Junia, Tryphaena, Tryphosa, Persis, the mother of Rufus, Julia and the sister of Nereus.
